summary: An informational report documenting how the requirements for advancing a routing protocol to Full Standard have been met for OSPF version 2. It collects evidence on implementations and interoperability.

plainLanguage.summary: A school report showing that a map-sharing system for routers did everything required to earn its top grade.

questions: how did ospfv2 become a full standard
subtitle: A report showing how OSPF version 2 routing protocol met all requirements to become a Full Internet Standard.

tldr.problem: OSPF version 2 was a successful routing protocol widely used by Internet Service Providers, but it needed to prove it met the Internet's formal criteria for advancing to Full Standard status.
tldr.mechanism: This report documents how OSPF met the standardization requirements: it lists protocol improvements since becoming a Draft Standard, provides implementation and interoperability evidence from multiple vendors, shows real-world deployment data, and describes security mechanisms.
tldr.outcome: OSPF was successfully promoted to Full Standard (RFC 2328) in April 1998, recognized as a mature, thoroughly tested, and widely deployed routing protocol suitable for production Internet use.

today: RFC 2329 is an Informational RFC that documents OSPF version 2's achievement of Full Standard status in April 1998. OSPF remains a Full Internet Standard today and continues to be widely deployed in enterprise networks and service provider networks worldwide, although newer protocols like IS-IS are also used for similar purposes. The protocol has remained remarkably stable since 1998, with RFC 2328 still serving as the authoritative standard specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) is an interior gateway protocol used by routers within a single organization to share information about the network's topology (its physical layout and connections). OSPF is a link-state protocol, meaning each router maintains a complete map of the entire network, computes the shortest path to every destination, and quickly adapts when the network changes.

This RFC documents how OSPF version 2 (OSPFv2) satisfied the formal criteria for becoming a Full Internet Standard. It demonstrates that OSPF has been implemented by multiple independent vendors, successfully interoperates between those implementations, is widely deployed in production networks, and has proper security mechanisms. These criteria ensure that a protocol is mature and trustworthy before it earns Full Standard status.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers use OSPF to share maps of the network with each other so they know where to send data. This RFC proves OSPF works well enough to be an official Internet standard.

sections.title: OSPF Features and Design
sections.content:
OSPF provides several important capabilities for modern routing. It responds quickly to topology changes, using minimal network bandwidth compared to older protocols like RIP. It supports CIDR addressing, the efficient IP address allocation scheme. OSPF exchanges can be authenticated to ensure routers only trust routing information from authorized peers. The protocol supports equal-cost multipath, allowing traffic to be distributed across multiple equivalent routes.

OSPF can divide an Autonomous System into areas, creating a two-level routing hierarchy that reduces the amount of routing traffic. It also allows import of external routing information (learned from other routing protocols), with a tagging mechanism to exchange additional information at AS boundaries. These features make OSPF both powerful and flexible for large networks.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF lets routers quickly notice when the network changes, use efficient addresses, check that messages are real, and organize large networks into smaller sections.

sections.title: Enhancements Since Draft Standard
sections.content:
OSPF became a Draft Standard with RFC 1583 in March 1994. Since then, the protocol was refined and two major features were added. The protocol's flooding algorithm was improved to handle low-speed links better, resolve database synchronization issues, prevent unnecessary retransmissions, and rate-limit responses to outdated link state advertisements.

Two significant new capabilities were added after Draft Standard status: the Point-to-MultiPoint interface allows OSPF to run over non-broadcast networks (like satellite links) without requiring every router to connect to every other router directly, making OSPF more flexible. Cryptographic Authentication allows routers to verify each OSPF message using keyed message digest algorithms (such as MD5), protecting against spoofed routing updates. Interoperability between multiple vendors was demonstrated for both features, with at least six Point-to-MultiPoint implementations and three Cryptographic Authentication implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Since 1994, OSPF was improved to handle difficult networks better and two new features were added: a way to work on non-direct links and a way to sign messages so routers know they are real.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment Data
sections.content:
The RFC presents evidence of widespread OSPF implementation and deployment. A questionnaire sent to the OSPF mailing list in January 1996 received twelve responses from eleven router vendors and one test equipment manufacturer, representing six independent implementations. The response data shows: OSPF areas and stub areas were implemented and interoperated in 10 out of 10 responding implementations; virtual links in 10 implementations (with 9 able to interoperate); equal-cost multipath in 10 implementations (7 interoperating); and NBMA (non-broadcast multi-access) support in 9 implementations.

Testing data demonstrates that vendors had tested OSPF with up to 1600 routers in a domain and 30,000 external routes. Real-world deployment data from January 1998 showed OSPF in networks as large as 1000 routers in a domain. Four vendors estimated a combined 182,000 OSPF routers in service worldwide, organized into 4,300 separate OSPF routing domains. This level of implementation diversity and deployment scale directly satisfies the standardization criteria.
sections.plainLanguage: Survey answers showed that many different companies had built OSPF, they could all talk to each other, and thousands of real networks were using OSPF successfully.

sections.title: Protocol Security and Authentication
sections.content:
OSPF supports multiple authentication types that can be configured per network segment. All OSPF protocol exchanges are authenticated, meaning every router verifies the source of routing information it receives. The simplest authentication type is a plaintext password, but this provides only basic protection.

The Cryptographic Authentication type is considered secure against passive attacks (eavesdropping) and provides significant protection against active attacks (message injection or modification). When enabled, each router appends a message digest (computed using MD5 and a shared secret key) to its transmitted OSPF packets. Receiving routers verify the digest to confirm that the packet is authentic and has not been tampered with. However, cryptographic authentication does not provide confidentiality (the messages are still readable) and does not protect against traffic analysis. Key management is also outside the scope of the OSPF protocol itself.
sections.plainLanguage: OSPF can use secret signatures on messages so routers know they are talking to real routers, not imposters.

sections.title: Path to Full Standard Status
sections.content:
The standardization process for routing protocols is defined in RFC 1264. To advance from Draft Standard to Full Standard requires demonstrating that the protocol is mature, widely implemented, thoroughly tested, and operationally viable. This RFC provides all required evidence: multiple independent implementations from different vendors, demonstrated interoperability between those implementations, real-world deployment at scale, and documented security mechanisms.

The report fulfills the formal documentation requirement by analyzing OSPF's achievements against the standardization criteria. The publication of this report in April 1998 accompanied the publication of RFC 2328, which is the authoritative specification for OSPF version 2 at Full Standard level. The clear evidence of maturity and widespread adoption justified OSPF's advancement to the highest standardization level.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC shows that OSPF has been tested enough and is used widely enough to become an official Full Standard for routing.
